name: Setipiprant
lead: Setipiprant (ACT-129968, later KYTH-105) is an investigational oral drug that selectively blocks the DP2 (CRTH2) receptor for prostaglandin D2.[1][4] It was developed by Actelion for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis, then taken up for androgenetic alopecia (male pattern hair loss) after a 2012 finding that PGD2 is elevated in balding scalp and inhibits hair growth.[1][13]

The appeal for hair is the proposed mechanism: if PGD2 signalling holds follicles back in balding scalp, blocking its receptor could in principle help preserve or regrow hair, without acting on androgens the way finasteride does. This made it one of the best-known non-hormonal candidates in the hair-loss field.[1][18]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial in men with androgenetic alopecia finished in 2018 without a statistically significant improvement over placebo, according to Wikipedia.[1][3] The drug is not approved for any use.

paras: Setipiprant was identified as a potent, selective, orally bioavailable CRTH2 antagonist in a 2013 medicinal chemistry paper from the Actelion programme, which describes it as a clinical development candidate for asthma and seasonal allergic rhinitis; the starting point was an earlier benzoyl pyridoindole acetic acid CRTH2 antagonist.[5] Its molecular formula is C24H19FN2O3 and it is a light yellow to yellow solid.[1] The principal route of metabolism, oxidation of the naphthoyl group, was verified through synthesis of proposed metabolites.[19]

PGD2 acts through DP1, CRTH2 (DP2) and TP receptors; CRTH2 mediates migration and activation of Th2 lymphocytes, eosinophils and basophils.[6] Setipiprant binds DP2 with a dissociation constant of about 6 nM and does not block the thromboxane receptor, according to Wikipedia.[1] In hair, Garza and colleagues reported in 2012 that PGD2 inhibits hair growth and is elevated in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia, as is the enzyme that produces it, PTGDS; this suggested that blocking DP2 could counter the signal.[1][13] A 2017 paper asked whether inhibition of aldose reductase contributes to setipiprant's anti-inflammatory action.[17]

Human studies describe its tolerability, pharmacokinetics, metabolism and formulation bioavailability.[7][8][16] Peak plasma levels occur about 1.8 to 4 hours after an oral dose, the half-life is about 11 hours, and tablet and capsule forms are bioequivalent.[1] An interaction study with simvastatin in 22 healthy men found the simvastatin profile was similar with and without setipiprant, consistent with weak CYP3A4 induction.[14] A modelling study compared receptor internalisation blockade with another CRTH2 antagonist to inform dose selection.[15]

Actelion developed setipiprant for allergic disease; development for asthma stopped as it offered no clear advantage over existing drugs, though it was described as well tolerated and reasonably effective at reducing allergen-induced airway responses.[1][2] A review of DP2 antagonists lists setipiprant among compounds with unpromising outcomes in asthma.[4]

After the 2012 PGD2 finding in balding scalp, Kythera acquired the rights to setipiprant for hair loss; Allergan acquired Kythera in 2015 and continued development.[1] The phase 2 alopecia trial began in July 2016 and completed in 2018.[1][12]

In allergic asthmatics, setipiprant reduced allergen-induced airway responses in a double-blind crossover study.[2] Phase 2 and 3 seasonal allergic rhinitis studies in Texas over two weeks reported efficacy and safety results.[9] Registered trials include a phase 2 asthma study (n=438) and a phase 3 rhinitis study (n=630).[10][11] Phase 2 and 3 trials were reported by Wikipedia as showing no severe adverse effects and no pattern different from placebo.[1]

A phase 2a trial (NCT02781311) enrolled 169 men aged 18 to 49 with androgenetic alopecia; 74 received placebo, 83 setipiprant twice daily and 12 finasteride 1 mg daily, the finasteride group having been removed by protocol amendment and summarised without statistical testing. Coprimary endpoints were change in target area hair count and blinded subject self-assessment of photographs, with a 24-week treatment period and week 32 follow-up. About 69 percent completed the week 24 visit.[3][12] Wikipedia reports that the trial did not show a statistically significant improvement over placebo.[1] A review of new alopecia drugs places setipiprant among emerging approaches.[18]

Setipiprant is discussed in hair-loss communities as a notable PGD2-pathway candidate that was tested in a controlled trial; it is not marketed, and it is an investigational compound without a regulatory approval for hair loss or any other use.[1]

timeline.event: PGD2 reported elevated in balding scalp; Kythera acquires setipiprant.[1][13]
Phase 2a trial concludes without significant benefit.[1]

card.summary: PGD2-receptor blocker that came from allergy research to hair loss, and did not beat placebo in its phase 2a trial.
card.note: Never approved; hair trial reported no significant benefit.

quick.overview:
Setipiprant is an experimental oral drug that blocks the PGD2 receptor CRTH2. It was developed for asthma and hay fever, then tested for male pattern hair loss.

The phase 2a hair trial did not show a statistically significant improvement over placebo.
quick.mechanism: Blocks CRTH2 (DP2) so PGD2, which is elevated in balding scalp, cannot signal through it.
quick.risks: Early trials reported no severe adverse effects distinguishable from placebo; it is unapproved and not marketed.

chain: Counters a hair-growth inhibitor that is elevated in balding scalp
Proposed to preserve or regrow scalp hair
angle.text: Setipiprant was tested as an oral drug to stop PGD2 from suppressing hair follicles in men with androgenetic alopecia. It is not marketed, and people interested in it follow it as a research-stage hair-loss pathway.
